quiz.q: How does the enlightened model of representation differ fundamentally from the delegate model?
options: It requires representatives to strictly obey instructions given by their local voters during elections.
It grants representatives autonomy to act for the national interest rather than following strict voter mandates.
It eliminates legislative deliberation in favor of frequent citizen referendums on daily administrative policies.
It selects representatives through proportional list systems rather than single-member majoritarian constituencies.
quiz.why: According to Burke and Mill, representatives in the enlightened model exercise autonomous judgment for the nation rather than acting as bound delegates.

quiz.q: According to Nancy Fraser, why do marginalized sections of society need to create counter-publics?
options: To replace open public deliberation with centralized bureaucratic watchdog commissions.
To enforce strict majoritarian quotas that eliminate the need for independent civic activism.
To build alternative public spheres where they can articulate concerns free from dominant group domination.
To withdraw completely from political life and avoid engaging with wider governance issues.
quiz.why: Fraser argued that marginalized groups need their own discursive spaces to debate needs and challenge domination by powerful groups.

quiz.q: Why did Aristotle consider collective citizen deliberation superior to governance by expert rulers acting alone?
options: Ordinary citizens deliberating together can pool diverse insights to reach better decisions than isolated experts.
Majoritarian headcounts naturally produce virtuous outcomes without requiring reasoned debate or discussion.
Philosopher-kings inevitably adhere to rigid voter mandates that restrict administrative flexibility.
Voting without prior deliberation prevents factional conflict and speeds up legislative decisions.
quiz.why: Aristotle maintained that citizens deliberating collectively combine their knowledge, producing sounder outcomes than individual experts.

quiz.q: What constitutes the core requirement of Jürgen Habermas's ideal speech situation?
options: Decisions are settled through rapid majoritarian balloting to prevent deadlock among competing interests.
Government authorities determine speaking eligibility to keep public debate aligned with state policy.
Only recognized subject-matter experts are permitted to propose solutions during civic assemblies.
All participants enjoy equal speaking rights and agreements are guided solely by the force of argument.
quiz.why: Habermas specifies that in an ideal speech situation, participants engage as equals where no pressure exists except the force of argument.
